title: Brick structures from Eastern Vidarbha during 5th to 8th Century CE
author_affiliation: UGC NET, Contributory Lecturer, Dept of Ancient Indian History Culture & Archaeology, RTM Nagpur University, Nagpur
publisher: Directorate of Culture and Archaeology, Government of Chhattisgarh, Raipur
region: Eastern Vidarbha (Mandhal, Mansar, Nagardhan, Pauni, Hamlapuri)
abstract: Brick as a building material is used traditionally, produced in numerous classes, types, materials, and sizes, which vary with region and time, and are produced in bulk. Two basic categories of bricks are fired and non-fired bricks. Fired bricks are one of the longest-lasting and strongest building materials, sometimes referred to as artificial stone, and have been used since circa 4000 BCE. This paper provides an extensive survey and architectural analysis of 5th to 8th Century CE brick temples, stupas, monasteries, and fortification structures across Eastern Vidarbha, examining construction bonds, clay compositions, mortar types, and historical preservation challenges.
highlights: Comprehensive documentation of monumental brick remains across Nagpur, Bhandara, and Chandrapur districts.
Analysis of brick bonding patterns (English bond, Flemish variations) and mortar compositions in ancient Deccan architecture.
Comparison of ritualistic brick platforms and sanctums from the Pravarapura-Nandivardhana branch of the Vakatakas.
Detailed structural measurements and analysis of surviving brick courses across key archaeological mounds.

title: A Fragmentary Lajjā Gaurī Image from Brahmapuri, Dist. Chandrapur
author_affiliation: Former Professor & Head, Dept. of AIHC&A, RTM Nagpur University & Contributory Lecturer, Dept of AIHC&A, RTM Nagpur University
publisher: Directorate of Culture and Archaeology, Government of Chhattisgarh, Raipur
period: Early Historic to Medieval (Cult origins from 3rd C CE)
abstract: Lajjā Gaurī is a goddess associated with abundance and fertility, euphemistically described as Lajjā ('modesty'). Lajjā Gaurī is a form of Devī who is known by many other names such as Aditi in the Rig Veda—the Primal Mother of the Gods and Goddesses, of the Universe, and of all that lives. Some of Her most famous images are found at Kudavelli Sangameshvara Temple, Badami Museum, and Ellora. This research paper highlights the prevailing cult of Lajjā Gaurī in Vidarbha through a rare fragmentary stone image discovered at Brahmapuri in Chandrapur district, analyzing iconographic posture, symbolic lotus motifs, and regional distribution across Nagardhan, Pauni, Paunar, and Ramtek.
highlights: Discovery and detailed iconographic cataloging of a rare fragmentary Lajjā Gaurī sculpture from Brahmapuri.
Comparative analysis with known sites across the Deccan: Kudavelli, Badami, Alampur, Ellora, and Ter.
Contextualization of the fertility cult evolution from early aniconic pot-forms to anthropomorphic depictions.
Detailed mapping of Lajjā Gaurī findspots in eastern and northern Maharashtra.

title: Revisiting Vidarbha Megalithic Material Culture – Study of some Tools and Implements found from various Excavations in Vidarbha
author_affiliation: Contributory Lecturer, Department of Ancient Indian History, Culture & Archaeology, RTM Nagpur University, Nagpur
journal: ICON Journal of Archaeology and Culture
publisher: Wakankar Rock Art and Heritage Welfare Society, Bhopal in association with B.R. Publishing Corporation, Delhi
issue: In Honor of Prof. J.N. Pal
period: Iron Age Megalithic Period (c. 1000 BCE - 300 BCE)
region: Eastern Vidarbha (Junapani, Mahurjhari, Naikund, Khairwada, Takalghat, Bhagimohari)
abstract: The entire Vidarbha, especially its Eastern part, is dotted with Megalithic Iron Age burials (Stone Circles) as well as habitation sites, explored, recorded, and excavated from time to time. This paper revisits the material culture unearthed from premier Vidarbha sites, providing a systematic typological and metallurgical study of iron and copper implements. It categorizes tools into agricultural implements (hoes, sickles, ploughshares), household items (knives, ladles, cauldrons), weapons of offence and defence (swords, daggers, arrowheads, spears), and equine equipment (horse bits, stirrups, bells), shedding light on early iron technology and social stratification.
highlights: Systematic functional classification of over 50 distinct types of iron and copper implements from Vidarbha stone circles.
Assessment of the revolutionary Naikund iron smelting furnace and indigenous smelting technology.
Analysis of equestrian gear demonstrating the advanced horse-riding warrior pastoralist-agrarian economy.
Distribution maps correlating stone circle clusters with rich mineral deposits and ancient trade conduits.

title: A Comparative Study of Material Culture found from Excavations at Bhokardan and Paunar
author_affiliation: Dept of Ancient Indian History, Culture & Archaeology, RTM Nagpur University
journal: Human and Heritage: An Archaeological Spectrum of Asiatic Countries (Felicitation to Prof Ajith Kumar)
publisher: New Bharatiya Book Corporation, Delhi / University of Kerala
period: Satavahana to Post-Satavahana / Vakataka Period (c. 2nd C BCE - 6th C CE)
abstract: Archaeological excavations bring forth the material and cultural history of a site. During ancient times, geographically separated locations maintained strong cultural, social, and economic connections via trans-regional trade routes. This paper presents a rigorous comparative evaluation of excavated finds from two landmark ancient cities of Maharashtra: Bhokardan (ancient Bhogavardhana in Marathwada) and Paunar (ancient Pravarapura in Vidarbha). Both were flourishing centers under the Satavahanas and Vakatakas. The study compares ceramic assemblages (Rouletted ware, Red Polished ware), terracotta art (including ivory figurines and bullae), coins, and beads to map regional exchange dynamics.
highlights: Direct comparative matrix between the stratigraphy and cultural sequences of Bhokardan and Paunar.
Analysis of ivory craftsmanship, Roman influence, and terracotta bullae representing international exchange.
Identification of overland trading routes linking Ujjain, Tagara (Ter), Bhogavardhana, and Paunar.
Evaluation of ceramic technology and metallurgical standardization during the early centuries CE.

title: A Study of Some Celestial Events Missed by Ancient Indians
author_affiliation: Lecturer, Dept. of AIHC & Archaeology, RTM Nagpur University, Nagpur
period: Ancient to Medieval Periods (c. 5000 BCE to 1604 CE)
abstract: Every 50 years or so, a star in our Galaxy blows itself apart in a supernova explosion, producing spectacular celestial phenomena bright enough to catch the attention of early observers centuries before the invention of the telescope. While Chinese, Arab, European, and Japanese astronomers kept meticulous chronicle records of historical guest stars (such as SN 1006, SN 1054 Crab Nebula supernova, Tycho's Nova of 1572, and Kepler's Supernova of 1604), explicit records in ancient Indian Sanskrit astronomical treatises are remarkably scarce or cryptic. This paper critically examines why these events were overlooked, unrecorded, or obscured in myth, analyzing astronomical passages, Kashmir rock art engravings, and observational paradigms of Vedic and Siddhantic astronomy.
highlights: In-depth examination of the 4 historic supernovae visible to the naked eye (SN 1006, SN 1054, SN 1572, SN 1604) against Indian chronology.
Detailed analysis of the Burzahom (Kashmir) Neolithic rock art hunting scene as a plausible representation of a dual-sun/supernova event.
Critical investigation into why Siddhantic texts prioritized planetary motions and eclipses over ephemeral transient phenomena.
Comprehensive comparison between Indian astronomical records and contemporary Chinese Han/Song imperial dynastic annals.

title: Some Historic Sites in Nagpur District- Present Status
author_affiliation: Lecturer, Dept. of AIHC & Archaeology, RTM Nagpur University, Nagpur
region: Nagpur District (Ambala-Talao, Bhugaon, Bhuyari, Khopadi, Vena, Wadoda)
abstract: Heritage is an indispensable part of our identity, and heritage conservation is viewed as a subject of utmost importance for national identity and preserving ancient knowledge and arts. While prominent monuments receive state patronage, numerous regional historic sites remain neglected due to lack of local awareness, developmental encroachments, and insufficient resources. This research paper presents an on-ground status report of neglected archaeological sites in Nagpur district, including ancient step wells (baolis), Hemadpanthi stone temples, Megalithic stone circles, and medieval water conservation reservoirs, advocating urgent conservation protocols under statutory frameworks.
highlights: Extensive photographic documentation and GPS location survey of neglected historical landmarks in Nagpur district.
Architectural analysis of Hemadpanthi dry-masonry techniques at Bhuyari and Bhugaon temples.
Assessment of human encroachment and ecological degradation threatening ancient step wells and water heritage.
Policy recommendations and community stewardship models aligned with UNESCO heritage guidelines and Article 51A(f) of the Indian Constitution.

title: A Vishnu Sculpture from Kelzar, District Wardha, Maharashtra
author_affiliation: Department of Ancient Indian History, Culture and Archaeology, R.T.M. Nagpur University, Nagpur
journal: Heritage: Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies in Archaeology
period: Medieval Period / Yadava Dynasty (c. 12th–13th Century CE)
abstract: Vishnu is the most revered deity of the Hindu pantheon, possessing cult followers globally across Vaishnavite traditions, Bhagavata worship, the Krishna cult, and the Varkari pantheon. This paper examines an exquisite stone image of Lord Vishnu discovered at the ancient site of Kelzar in Wardha district, Maharashtra. Kelzar, historically renowned for its ancient mounds and connection with the Mahabharata's Ekachakranagari, yielded this beautifully carved deity holding classical ayudhas (attributes). The sculpture is meticulously classified according to canonical iconography laid out in texts such as Rupamandana and Agni Purana.
highlights: Iconometric and stylistic analysis of the four-armed standing (sthanaka) Vishnu sculpture of Kelzar.
Canonical identification of the 24 forms (Chaturvimshati-murti) of Vishnu based on permutation of the four attributes.
Study of ornamentation, kirita-mukuta, vanamala, and parivara-devatas carved in basalt rock.
Historical association of Kelzar with Mahabharata lore and medieval trade conduits connecting Vidarbha.

title: Paleolithic Tools in Nagpur: Recent Discovery
author_affiliation: Lecturer, Dept. of AIHC & Archaeology, RTM Nagpur University, Nagpur
region: Nagpur City & Surrounds (Nag River basin, Seminary Hills / Ambazari)
abstract: Eastern Maharashtra (Vidarbha) has long been known for prehistoric human antiquity, with Acheulian tool sites dated up to two million years ago such as Papamiya-Tekdi in Chandrapur district. This paper documents the unprecedented discovery of Paleolithic stone tools within Nagpur city urban territory. The article details the techno-typological attributes of the lithic assemblage—including Acheulian hand axes, cleavers, side scrapers, and discoidal cores crafted from local quartzite, chert, and chalcedony—and performs a comparative techno-morphological study with known Wardha-Wainganga basin paleolithic industries.
highlights: First formal publication documenting in-situ Lower and Middle Paleolithic tools discovered inside Nagpur urban limits.
Morphometric classification and flake-scar analysis of bifacial handaxes, scrapers, and cleavers.
Stratigraphical correlation of tool-bearing gravel beds with ancient pleistocene alluvial formations of the Nag and Wainganga rivers.
Comparative analysis establishing continuity between Nagpur discoveries and classic Acheulian horizons of Central India.
